overview.title: Event overview
overview.content: On 24 June 2026 at around 18:04-18:05 local time (2204-2205 UTC), two major earthquakes struck north-central Venezuela about 39-40 seconds apart: a magnitude 7.2 foreshock (initially reported as 7.1) near San Felipe/Morón, Carabobo-Yaracuy, followed by a magnitude 7.5 mainshock near Yumare, Veroes, Yaracuy, with USGS later locating the second epicentre about 17 km west of Catia La Mar, off La Guaira state. The mainshock was shallow (about 10 km depth), generating very strong to violent shaking (peak intensity approaching MMI 9) along the Boconó-Morón-El Pilar fault system at the Caribbean-South American plate boundary. USGS and media sources describe it as Venezuela's strongest recorded earthquake in more than 125 years. Shaking was felt across Caracas, La Guaira, Miranda, Carabobo, Aragua, Yaracuy, Falcón and other states, and as far as Colombia, the Caribbean and northern Brazil; a brief Caribbean tsunami advisory was cancelled within about an hour. The Government of Venezuela declared a National State of Emergency the same day and designated La Guaira, the most affected state, as a disaster zone.

hazards.title: Hazard and cascading hazards
hazards.content: The primary hazard was the twin shallow earthquakes (M7.2 and M7.5) with a USGS PAGER alert of Orange for the foreshock and Red for the mainshock, indicating high probable casualties and extensive damage. Aftershock sequences were intense and prolonged: OCHA reported more than 302 aftershocks by 26 June, FEWS NET and UNFPA reported over 600 and then nearly 1,000 by early July, CESVI reported over 1,300 by 20 July, and IFRC reported 1,463 aftershocks by 6 August; USGS estimated a 40% chance of a magnitude 6+ aftershock in the first week. Notable aftershocks included a magnitude 5.1 event near Tucacas (Falcón) on the night of 25 June and a magnitude 4.4 event northeast of Guatire (Miranda) in the early hours of 26 June. The Shelter Cluster/UNHCR flagged secondary hazard risk from heavy rains and landslides/mudflows as the region entered its annual rainfall peak, compounded by seismic destabilisation of slopes, requiring landslide mapping. PAHO also flagged risk of disease outbreaks (vaccine-preventable diseases, acute diarrheal disease, vector-borne diseases) as a cascading public health hazard linked to displacement and damaged WASH infrastructure.

exposure_vulnerability.title: Exposure and vulnerability
exposure_vulnerability.content: UNDP's RAPIDA assessment estimated about 8.6 million people exposed to above-moderate shaking across northern Venezuela, including 2.1 million exposed to stronger shaking, and 1.7 million structures in affected areas. The earthquakes struck a densely populated corridor including Caracas and coastal cities, hitting a country already classified 24th of 97 crises on the INFORM Severity Index (high severity, 7.6/10) due to prolonged economic and political crisis (ACAPS). REACH's pre-crisis Humanitarian Situation Monitoring found Aragua, La Guaira, Carabobo and Falcón had the weakest pre-earthquake conditions in shelter, water access and health services; in La Guaira, 62% of the population lived in fragile housing with repair needs, poverty stood at 94% and multidimensional poverty at 46% (ACAPS). ACAPS also noted widespread lack of enforcement of modern earthquake building codes, substandard construction materials, informal settlements on unstable hillsides, and a health system in protracted collapse with pre-existing shortages of vaccines, personnel and medicines. IRC noted roughly 8 million Venezuelans had emigrated in recent years, leaving workforce gaps that constrained search-and-rescue and recovery capacity, and nearly 8 million people were already in humanitarian need before the earthquakes.

impacts.title: Impacts
impacts.content: Casualty figures rose steadily across sources: 32 dead/~700 injured (initial, 25 June, Acting President Delcy Rodríguez), 164 dead/971 injured (25 June, Data Friendly Space), 589 dead/2,980 injured (26 June, REACH), 920 dead/3,360 injured (26 June, OCHA Sitrep 3), 1,423 infrastructures affected (OCHA, 26 June), 1,430 dead/3,230 injured (29 June, MSF), 1,719 dead/5,034 hospitalised/15,866 affected (29 June, UNHCR), 1,700 dead/5,000 injured/15,800 displaced (29 June, FEWS NET), 3,342 dead/16,470 injured (5 July, UNFPA/OCHA Sitrep 12), 3,535 dead/16,740 injured and over 2,500 damaged infrastructure sites including 38 hospitals (6 July, IOM), 4,490 dead/16,740 injured/17,907 homeless (two weeks post-event, UNICEF), 5,208 dead/16,740 injured/856 affected buildings/17,907 homeless (20 July, CESVI), and 5,546 dead/16,740 injured/6,462 rescued alive (31 July, ChildFund). PAHO's 10 July analysis cites the 5 July figures of 3,342 deaths, 16,740 injuries, 6,462 rescued and 17,345 displaced. IFRC's July 1 brief notes tens of thousands reported missing with ambiguous figures across sources, and USGS modelling giving a 50% chance final casualties fall between 1,000-10,000 and 30% chance they exceed 10,000. UNHCR reported (29 June) 2,501 damaged infrastructure sites including 774 housing units and 38 hospitals, with 189 housing units completely collapsed. Economic estimates vary: UNDP's RAPIDA (26 June) estimated US$6.7 billion in direct physical damage (~6% of GDP); FEWS NET (6 July) cited preliminary assessments of US$4.7-8.7 billion; UNDRR's analytical estimate (3 July) put total direct physical damage at US$37 billion (US$24 billion to buildings, US$13 billion to infrastructure), a figure also cited by IRC. Key infrastructure disruptions included closure of Maiquetía/Simón Bolívar International Airport, suspension of Caracas Metro and railways, and power, water and telecommunications outages in multiple states.

prevention.title: Prevention and mitigation
prevention.content: Documents report no earthquake-resistant retrofitting or effective building-code enforcement prior to the event. ACAPS states that most buildings across Venezuela are unlikely to have been built in line with modern earthquake regulations, with reports indicating a lack of enforcement of building standards, resulting in higher likelihood of homes becoming uninhabitable or structurally compromised. No risk financing, land-use planning or mitigation works prior to the earthquake are mentioned in the documents.

preparedness.title: Preparedness
preparedness.content: The documents do not describe specific pre-event early warning systems, contingency plans, drills or stockpiles for earthquakes in Venezuela. FUNVISIS (Venezuela's seismological institute) is cited only as an information source in Health Cluster reports, not as having issued pre-event warnings. A brief Caribbean tsunami advisory was issued and cancelled within about an hour of the mainshock, indicating some regional monitoring capacity, but no national earthquake early warning system is referenced. Venezuela lacked emergency shelters prior to the earthquakes, according to ACAPS, forcing reliance on repurposed buildings not designed to host displaced populations.

response.title: Response
response.content: Search and rescue operations were activated immediately by the Venezuelan Red Cross and other national responders in the Capital District on 24 June, and the government declared a National State of Emergency the same day, designating La Guaira as a disaster zone. IFRC allocated CHF 2 million in DREF on 25 June and the first international search and rescue and humanitarian teams arrived that day; a qualitative damage and needs assessment was conducted in La Guaira. On 26 June, IFRC launched a CHF 50 million Emergency Appeal (Federation-wide CHF 55 million), a field hospital was installed at Jorge García Carmeiro Stadium, and a Field Operations Centre established; the UNDAC team and USAR teams under INSARAG coordination were already present. The Expanded Health Cluster met with the Ministry of Popular Power for Health (MPPS) on 26 June to consolidate a single response mechanism; temporary access restrictions to La Guaira were imposed from the night of 26 June to prioritise search and rescue. PAHO's Strategic Reserve in Panama dispatched 4 tons of medical and field supplies, provided the Ministry of Health with medical-surgical supplies and body bags, and coordinated 320 body bags and 3 refrigerated containers for body management by 30 June; Colombia's Ministry of Health and Social Protection mobilised 646 kg of medical supplies via PAHO/UNGRD/Colombian Red Cross. By 6 July, Turkish Red Crescent reported responding to the disaster. UNHCR scaled up protection and shelter support, seeking US$14.85 million for 30,000 people, and supported government-led multi-service centres. IOM, UNICEF (requiring US$65.7 million to reach 470,000 people), UNFPA (seeking US$10 million for 64,000 people), MSF, Project HOPE, CESVI, Good Neighbors and ChildFund all mobilised emergency assistance. Private sector contributions reached US$32.9 million from 27 partners by 9 July (OCHA/CBi), and Canada matched CAD 7 million in public donations. Constraints included debris-blocked roads in Caracas, Yaracuy and Carabobo, damage to Maiquetía airport, telecommunications disruption, power outages and suspended gas services, and workforce shortages due to prior emigration (IRC). By around 7 July, Project HOPE reported search-and-rescue operations winding down nationally, and by 31 July ChildFund reported rescuers no longer searching for survivors and international USAR teams scaling back.

recovery.title: Recovery and reconstruction
recovery.content: By early-mid July 2026 the response was described as transitioning from emergency to early recovery: Project HOPE (7 July) reported debris clearance, condemnation of damaged buildings for demolition, and municipal civil protection teams conducting structural assessments with green/yellow/red habitability markings. OCHA issued an Addendum to the 2026 Humanitarian Response Plan (12 July) targeting 1.3 million earthquake-affected people across seven states, with associated logistics coordination needs budgeted at US$825,000. PAHO's 12 August Sitrep No.9 reported health service recovery advancing, with ICU and maternity capacity being restored at Hospital Dr. José Gregorio Hernández, rehabilitation planning in priority facilities, over 31,000 vaccine doses administered, and a USD 18 million Revolving Fund credit line supporting national vaccine supply security. IRC (22 July) warned that without urgent investment in local economies and livelihoods, Venezuela risked spiraling into deeper crisis, noting UNDRR's US$37 billion damage estimate and pre-existing extreme poverty affecting over half the population. CESVI (20 July) reported humanitarian actors planning assistance for 1.3 million people over six months, with over 23,000 people still in transitional camps. No detailed reconstruction plan, build-back-better framework or housing reconstruction programme is described in the documents.

needs_gaps.title: Needs and gaps
needs_gaps.content: The Health Cluster/PAHO (27 June) identified critical gaps in food, safe water, hygiene kits, non-food items, clothing and safe temporary shelter, alongside needs for logistical support, mental health and psychosocial support, and protection pathways for unaccompanied children. REACH (26 June) highlighted pre-existing water access problems and health system shortages of medicines, equipment and trained staff compounding needs. ChildFund's OCHA-based Rapid Needs Assessment (31 July) ranked priority needs as health (53%), safe water (52%), food security (50%), psychosocial support (27%), sanitation/hygiene (22%), protection/safety/dignity (18%) and shelter (17%). Project HOPE's needs assessment (July, published August) across 12-16 health facilities in La Guaira, Miranda and Distrito Capital found 43% of facilities with structural damage, 69% with suspended outpatient services, 81% with staff access difficulties, 63% with water interruptions and 56% with electricity interruptions, alongside gaps in emergency obstetric care, mental health/psychosocial support, water quality monitoring and protection mechanisms. UNFPA (7 August) reported 24,477 people in 107 transitional shelters facing overcrowding, limited privacy and inadequate lighting, heightening GBV risks for women and girls. UNHCR and ACAPS flagged that many displacement sites did not meet minimum protection standards. IFRC's Emergency Appeal remained only 29.1% funded of its CHF 50 million target as of 12 August, indicating a substantial funding gap.

lessons.title: Lessons and recommendations
lessons.content: ACAPS noted that censorship, limited transparency and restrictions on media and civil society have weakened public trust in official information, increasing reliance on informal networks, which is likely to hinder situational awareness, reduce effectiveness of risk communication, and complicate coordination between authorities, humanitarian responders and communities, delaying assistance delivery and targeting. IRC's analysis stressed that the pre-existing emigration of around 8 million Venezuelans created workforce gaps that constrained search-and-rescue capacity and will continue to limit early recovery, underscoring the need for urgent investment in local economies and livelihoods to prevent deeper crisis. The Shelter Cluster/UNHCR environmental note recommended applying Sphere Shelter Standard 7 and ECHO Minimum Environmental Requirements, including environmental impact assessments, sustainable materials, debris reuse/recycling, and monitoring of landslide and heavy rainfall risk, as guiding lessons for the ongoing shelter response.

confidence.title: Information quality
confidence.content: Documents span from the day of the event (25 June 2026) through mid-August 2026, providing a reasonably consistent and evolving picture, though casualty and damage figures diverge significantly across sources and over time, reflecting the fluid nature of a rapidly evolving emergency rather than clear contradictions. Core parameters (magnitudes 7.2 and 7.5, epicentre location, state of emergency, most-affected states) are consistent across nearly all sources. Economic loss estimates vary widely (US$6.7 billion UNDP RAPIDA vs US$37 billion UNDRR vs US$4.7-8.7 billion FEWS NET), reflecting different methodologies and scopes (direct damage only vs. broader estimates) rather than factual disagreement. Information on prevention and preparedness measures before the event is sparse, and no detailed reconstruction or long-term recovery plan is documented. Confidence in figures closer to the event (first 72 hours) is lower given explicit caveats in multiple reports that data were preliminary and subject to change.

passages.title: Venezuela Earthquake Situation Overview (25 June, 2026)
passages.text: On 24 June 2026, northern Venezuela was struck by two powerful earthquakes approximately 40 seconds apart - a magnitude 7.2 foreshock followed by a magnitude 7.5 mainshock, making it the country's strongest recorded earthquake in more than 125 years. The shallow earthquakes generated violent ground shaking across northern Venezuela, causing widespread damage to homes, health facilities, schools, transport infrastructure, and essential services. As of 25 June, at least 164 people have been confirmed dead and 971 injured, although casualty figures are expected to rise as search and rescue operations continue and assessments reach previously inaccessible areas. This report provides a consolidated overview of the evolving humanitarian situation, including the geographic extent of the earthquake and an assessment of the most affected states, municipalities, and parishes. It also analyses the humanitarian impacts in the context of Venezuela's pre-existing vulnerabilities, which are likely to compound the effects of the disaster and increase humanitarian needs. Drawing on available information, the report identifies priority humanitarian needs across key sectors, highlights the populations and locations facing the greatest risks, and outlines key response considerations and likely operational priorities to support emergency response, humanitarian coordination, and the transition towards early recovery. The methodology utilized in this report has been jointly developed with GiveDirectly.

passages.title: Good Neighbors Statement on the Venezuela Earthquake
passages.text: Good Neighbors expresses its deepest sympathy to the communities affected by the devastating earthquakes that struck Venezuela on 24 June 2026. The earthquakes caused widespread destruction to homes, public infrastructure, and essential services, leaving thousands of families in urgent need of humanitarian assistance. Families have lost loved ones, their homes, and their sense of safety. Children, in particular, are facing fear, uncertainty, and significant disruption to their daily lives. As aftershocks continue, many families remain displaced, taking shelter in cars, makeshift tents, and other temporary accommodations without reliable access to electricity, safe drinking water, food, or protection services. In response to this crisis, Good Neighbors is preparing an emergency response to protect the safety, well-being, and dignity of children and their families. Initial support is expected to include emergency shelter and other essential relief items, while additional assistance will be determined based on ongoing needs assessments and operational feasibility.

passages.text: **Situation Report No. 3** **Earthquakes in Venezuela** **26 June 2026** **Time: 3:00 pm** **Highlights** Two consecutive earthquakes of magnitude 7.2 and 7.5 on 24 June (18:00 local time); authorities report more than 302 aftershocks. Provisional official toll: 920 people dead and 3,360 injured; the figure continues to rise. More than 3,000 people resulted displaced, according to authorities. At least 1,423 infrastructures were affected; La Guaira remains the most affected state. Maiquetía International Airport closed without commercial flights; Caracas Metro and railways suspended; power outages in multiple states. International teams are already present in the country, including the United Nations Disaster Assessment and Coordination (UNDAC) team and Urban Search and Rescue (USAR) teams under INSARAG coordination. **Situation overview** Venezuela is facing a national emergency following the two consecutive high-magnitude earthquakes (7.2 and 7.5) of 24 June (18:00 local time) in the north-central region, with the epicentre off the coast some 28–30 km north-west of Montalbán (Carabobo). Authorities report more than 302 aftershocks, including a magnitude 5.1 event reported in Tucacas (Falcón state) on the night of 25 June, and a magnitude 4.4 aftershock northeast of Guatire (Miranda state) in the early hours of 26 June, sustaining high-risk conditions.

passages.title: Venezuela faces US$6.7 billion in economic losses from earthquakes, UNDP estimates
passages.text: **Caracas/New York, 26 June 2026** – The earthquakes that struck Venezuela on 24 June caused significant human suffering and loss of life, while also severely affecting livelihoods, infrastructure, and essential services. This includes a preliminary estimate of $6.7 billion in direct physical damage, equivalent to around 6% of GDP, according to a satellite-based Rapid Digital Assessment (RAPIDA) by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP). While the economic impact is substantial, the greatest loss is borne by the people and communities. The assessment is based on seismic modelling, satellite imagery and population data and was carried out in the hours after the quake. The quakes, measuring magnitude 7.2 and 7.5, hit near Venezuela’s northern coast and were felt across major population and economically important areas, including Caracas and the states of La Guaira, Carabobo, Miranda, Yaracuy, and Aragua. UNDP estimates that 1.7 million structures were in affected areas, including large numbers in the hardest-hit states. The analysis found that around 8.6 million people were exposed to above moderate shaking across the country’s north, including around 2.1 million exposed to stronger shaking.

passages.title: Venezuela June 2026 Earthquake: Emergency Situation Overview (26/06/2026)
passages.text: **KEY MESSAGES** On 24 June 2026, the largest earthquakes to strike Venezuela in over a century impacted an area with high levels of vulnerability after years of economic crisis. The most affected states entered the emergency with limited coping capacity. The earthquake struck areas where essential services were already operating under severe strain, limiting their capacity to absorb additional shocks. Across several affected states, HSM data indicated widespread housing deterioration, serious water access problems, and health systems facing shortages of medicines, equipment and trained staff. These pre-existing constraints are likely to amplify humanitarian needs as displacement and demand for services increase. The earthquake risks disrupting fragile livelihoods and reversing recent improvements in household food access. As food insecurity in Venezuela is primarily driven by limited purchasing power rather than market availability, households relying on daily labour, small businesses or informal income may see their ability to meet basic needs deteriorate rapidly, particularly where alternative coping mechanisms such as remittances or social assistance are limited. Pre-existing vulnerabilities suggest that humanitarian needs may be particularly severe in specific affected states rather than evenly distributed. HSM data indicate that Aragua, La Guaira, Carabobo and Falcón consistently reported some of the weakest pre-earthquake conditions across shelter, water access and health services, suggesting these areas may face greater challenges absorbing the impacts of the earthquake.

passages.text: The situation is characterized by a nationwide suspension of educational activities and significant infrastructure damage, with hundreds of schools affected, many declared unsafe, and an increasing use of schools as temporary shelters. Current efforts focus on rapid assessments, monitoring service disruption, and identifying needs for safe alternative learning spaces. While partners demonstrate strong operational capacity—including trained personnel for rapid deployment, delivery of socioemotional support and learning interventions, and the establishment of temporary learning spaces— available resources remain insufficient to meet the scale of needs. Existing capacities include education and recreational kits, temporary learning centre models, teacher training, WASH support, and dissemination of life-saving messages; however, significant additional funding is required to scale up these interventions and reach all affected children. Key priorities include establishing protective learning spaces, integrating socioemotional support, and progressively reintroducing essential learning, with ongoing coordination with shelter, protection, and WASH actors to ensure continuity of education and support the recovery of services. Security and access constraints The current operational environment in Venezuela presents challenges to humanitarian access following the June 24 earthquakes. Infrastructure collapse across Caracas, Yaracuy, and Carabobo has left roads blocked by debris, limiting mobility for rescue teams and humanitarian convoys. Damage to Maiquetia International Airport and disruptions in telecommunications further complicate logistics, delaying the arrival of relief supplies and restricting coordination.

They have caused widespread damage, with the cities of La Guaira and Caracas particularly affected. At least 1,430 people have died and 3,230 have been injured, according to the authorities.[1]( Search and rescue operations are still ongoing, even as the initial emergency trauma phase is coming to an end. Hospitals that were overwhelmed during the first days after the earthquakes are now receiving fewer patients. It is estimated that over 1,500 buildings were damaged, with most of them being residential. This has [displaced]( many families, who are now in need of shelter, [water and sanitation]( services, food, and medical care. ## How is MSF responding to the earthquakes in Venezuela?

passages.text: Families displaced from damaged or unsafe homes are staying with relatives, in streets and public spaces, and in churches, schools, stadiums and other improvised shelters. Many temporary sites do not yet meet minimum protection standards. UNHCR is supporting local authorities in set-up of government-led multi-service centres, while providing tools and equipment for the safe collection and management of information to identify protection needs, deliver protection services, and facilitate referrals to appropriate specialized services. UNHCR is scaling up support in two priority areas: protection and core relief items and shelter, and requires $14.8 million to support up to 30,000 earthquake-affected people over six months. Initial reports also indicate that a temporary accommodation site used for the reception of returnees in La Guaira was severely affected, underscoring the specific risks faced by people who were already in vulnerable situations prior to the earthquake. EMERGENCY UPDATE > Venezuela Earthquake Operational context On 24 June 2026, two consecutive high-magnitude earthquakes struck north-central Venezuela, severely affecting densely populated urban and coastal areas. La Guaira and the Greater Caracas area have reported the most significant impact, with damage also recorded in Miranda, Carabobo, Yaracuy, Falcón and Aragua. Multiple aftershocks continue to create risks for affected communities, further weaken damaged structures and complicate humanitarian operations. The earthquakes have caused extensive loss of life, injuries, displacement and disruption of essential services. Damage to electricity, water, telecommunications, roads, bridges, health facilities and the Simón Bolívar International Airport in Maiquetía has affected mobility, access to services and the operating environment for the response. In La Guaira, damage to key infrastructure has further constrained access to severely affected areas.

passages.title: Analytical estimate of damages caused by the June 24, 2026 earthquakes in Venezuela
sources: UN Office for Disaster Risk Reduction
passages.text: This document constitutes a first estimate of the direct physical damage, obtained through analytical modeling, of the effects caused by the earthquakes of June 24, 2026 in Venezuela. Its main purpose is to establish in a timely manner, an order of magnitude, technically supported, of the impact on buildings and infrastructure, however, it does not seek to provide a definitive quantification of the damages. The results indicate that damage to buildings (residential, commercial, educational, health, institutional and industrial) is estimated at around 3% of the total exposed stock (equivalent to $24,000 million US dollars), while damage to infrastructure (water and sanitation, telecommunications, roads, railways, energy, ports, airports, oil and gas) is estimated at around 4% of the total exposed stock (equivalent to $13,000 million US dollars). These values, totaling US$37,000 million US dollars, correspond exclusively to direct physical damage to buildings and infrastructure and do not include indirect economic losses, interruptions of productive activities and services, emergency response costs, effects on supply chains, social, environmental or macroeconomic impacts, or the costs associated with comprehensive recovery, structural retrofitting and reconstruction. For this reason, the total economic impact of the disaster is expected to be greater than the value of the direct damage estimated herein.

passages.text: Earthquakes in Venezuela Flash Update 26 June - 6 July 2026 Highlights Venezuela is facing a major humanitarian emergency following two powerful earthquakes of magnitudes 7.2 and 7.5 that struck the central-northern region of the country on 24 June. Nearly 1,000 aftershocks have been recorded, while search and rescue operations and humanitarian assistance continue across affected areas. Official reports indicate that at least 3,342 people have died and more than 16,470 have been injured.1 The states most affected remain La Guaira, Distrito Capital, Miranda, Carabobo, Yaracuy, Falcón and other neighbouring areas. More than 2,500 infrastructures have sustained damage, including 38 health facilities, while thousands of people remain displaced or accommodated in temporary shelters. The disruption of essential services, overcrowding in shelters, family separation and increased psychosocial distress are heightening protection risks, particularly for women, adolescent girls, persons with disabilities and older persons. Strengthening survivor-centred services and safe access to assistance remains an urgent priority. UNFPA is scaling up its life-saving sexual and reproductive health (SRH) and protection response to ensure continued access to maternal health services, emergency obstetric care, family planning, clinical management of rape, and gender-based violence (GBV) prevention and response. passages.text: **SITUATION OVERVIEW** On 24 June 2026, two powerful earthquakes measuring 7.2 and 7.5 struck the north-central region of the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela (henceforth referred to as Venezuela), triggering widespread devastation across several states, including La Guaira, Distrito Capital, Miranda, Carabobo, Aragua, and Falcón. The earthquakes, followed by hundreds of aftershocks, caused significant loss of life, with 3,535 people reported dead and over 16,740 injured, as of 6 July. Damage to more than 2,500 infrastructure assets, including 38 hospitals, has disrupted access to essential services, including healthcare, water supply, and transport systems, placing considerable strain on national response capacities. The disaster is unfolding in a context of pre-existing structural vulnerabilities, limited access to basic services, weakened public systems, and protracted humanitarian needs. As a result, the earthquakes have triggered an acute-on-chronic emergency, deepening existing vulnerabilities and increasing humanitarian needs across affected areas. Thousands of families have been displaced and are sheltering in collective centres (e.g. schools, sports centres), spontaneous settlements, self-managed sites, and open spaces due to the destruction or structural damage of homes and continued fear of further collapses. While initial response efforts by national authorities and international actors have focused on search and rescue, emergency medical assistance, and rapid assessments, significant gaps remain across key sectors.

passages.text: **CONTEXT** The Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela (hereinafter “Venezuela”) entered 2026 with pre-existing socioeconomic and humanitarian vulnerabilities that continue to affect population health and the resilience of essential services. Although some macroeconomic indicators showed modest improvement in recent years, millions of people continue to face difficulties accessing health care, safe water, food, and other basic services. These underlying conditions have increased the country's vulnerability to the health impacts of emergencies and disasters. On 24 June 2026, two powerful earthquakes of magnitude 7.2 and 7.5 struck northern Venezuela within less than one minute of each other, with epicentres located west of Caracas near the states of Yaracuy andCarabobo. The earthquakes generated very strong to violent ground shaking across a densely populated corridor, causing widespread damage to homes, health facilities, transport infrastructure, and essential services. As of 5 July 2026, official reports indicate more than 3,300 deaths, over 16,700 injuries, approximately 17,300 people displaced after losing their homes, and more than 6,400 people rescued. Three health facilities have been reported as damaged, while damage assessments continue in the affected areas. Numerous aftershocks followed the main event, further complicating emergency response and recovery efforts. This document provides a comprehensive assessment of the public health situation in Venezuela following the earthquakes of June 2026. It covers the context of the emergency, the impact on the population and health services, and an analysis of key health risks and priority actions for the humanitarian response.

Purpose This note summaries environmental policies and challenges associated with the response to the June 2026 Venezuela earthquakes. The information provided can be used to integrate environmental issues into plans and operations. This note focuses on shelter, formal and informal sheltering sites and housing, land and property (HLP), but is relevant for WASH-related efforts and activities involving infrastructure and energy as well. Weather and Hazard Overview: Heavy Rains and Landslides The impacted area is entering the normal annual peak in rainfall1 and can be affected by hurricanes or tropical low-pressure waves which can trigger intense rains. The potential for heavy rains needs to be monitored on a daily basis.2 In addition, landslide and mud flow mapping is needed, given a potential for increased events associated with seismic activity, as a results of heavy rains, or both.3 Experts in Venezuela can be expected to provide detailed technical support on these hazards.

passages.title: Venezuela Earthquake Response, July–December 2026 – Addendum to the 2026 UNICEF HAC Appeal
passages.text: On 24 June 2026, two powerful earthquakes of magnitude 7.2 and 7.5 struck north-central Venezuela, adding a new layer of humanitarian needs to an already fragile context. Two weeks after the earthquakes, official figures reported 4,490 deaths, 16,740 people injured and 17,907 people left without housing. The earthquakes have created a major child-focused humanitarian emergency on top of already significant needs. Children and families have lost homes, schools, access to safe water, health services, and protection systems, while aftershocks continue to heighten risks and complicate recovery. UNICEF requires **US$65.7 million to reach 470,000 people; of which 167,000 are children**. UNICEF’s earthquake response and is fully aligned with the addendum to the 2026 Humanitarian Response Plan (HRP) in Venezuela, which targets **1.3 million people affected by the earthquake** across 7 states. Before the earthquakes, UNICEF’s Humanitarian Action for Children (HAC) Appeal targeted 2.3 million people, including 1.2 million children, with a focus on addressing critical needs in health care, nutrition, safe water, sanitation, education, and child protection services.

passages.title: One month after earthquakes, Venezuela risks spiraling into deeper crisis without urgent investment in economic recovery
passages.text: Caracas, Venezuela, July 22, 2026 — Nearly one month after devastating twin earthquakes struck Venezuela on June 24, the window is closing to set the country on a sustainable path toward recovery. Without immediate investment in local economies and livelihood support, the disaster risks spiraling into a deeper humanitarian crisis, the International Rescue Committee (IRC) warns. Venezuela was already experiencing protracted economic instability long before the ground began to shake, with [over half of the population living in extreme poverty]( Years of economic hardship drove roughly 8 million people, mainly young adults, to leave the country. This has left a critical gap in the workforce that has impacted search and rescue efforts and will continue to constrain capacity as the vital early recovery phase begins. Now, the economic situation threatens to unravel further. An initial assessment by the United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR) estimates direct damage to housing and infrastructure to cost approximately $37 billion. Nearly 8 million people were in humanitarian need in Venezuela before the earthquakes.

passages.text: Needs Assessment Report: Venezuela Assessment findings on the state of health services and urgent humanitarian needs in La Guaira, Miranda, and Distrito Capital following the June 2026 earthquakes. July 2026 Following the June 2026 earthquakes in Venezuela, Project HOPE and its local subsidiary, Proyecto Esperanza, conducted a needs assessment across 12 health facilities and 160 households in Distrito Capital, Miranda, and La Guaira to evaluate health service capacity, WASH conditions, and community protection needs. The assessment found significant gaps in emergency obstetric care, mental health and psychosocial support services, water quality monitoring, handwashing infrastructure, and protection mechanisms, despite generally strong community knowledge of disease prevention and existing health system capacity. Findings indicate that humanitarian response efforts should prioritize restoring essential health supplies and infrastructure, strengthening WASH systems, expanding mental health and protection services, and addressing barriers that prevent communities and health facilities from translating existing knowledge into effective practices. On June 24, 2026, Venezuela was struck by a series of major earthquakes, triggering a humanitarian emergency in the north-central region of the country. The earthquakes caused significant damage to homes, health facilities, water systems, and transportation infrastructure, affecting the response capacity of communities and institutions.

passages.title: Needs Assessment Report: Venezuela - Assessment findings on the state of health services and urgent humanitarian needs in La Guaira, Miranda, and Distrito Capital following the June 2026 earthquakes (July 2026)
passages.text: On June 24, 2026, Venezuela was struck by a series of major earthquakes, triggering a humanitarian emergency in the north-central region of the country. The earthquakes caused significant damage to homes, health facilities, water systems, and transportation infrastructure, affecting the response capacity of communities and institutions. The emergency occurred against a backdrop of preexisting vulnerabilities: limited access to health services, deteriorated infrastructure, and shortages of medicines and medical supplies. These conditions exacerbated the impact of the disaster. To understand the initial impact on health services, Project HOPE, through its local subsidiary, Proyecto Esperanza, conducted a Rapid Needs Assessment at 16 health facilities in the states of La Guaira, Miranda, and Distrito Capital within 48 hours of the first earthquake. The findings revealed severe impacts: 43% of facilities sustained structural damage, 69% partially or completely suspended their outpatient services, and 81% reported difficulties in getting staff to their workplaces. All facilities reported an increase in demand for care, primarily due to traumatic injuries, hypertensive crises, and psychological stress. Water and electricity supplies were also affected: 63% of facilities reported interruptions in their water supply and 56% in electricity services.

passages.title: Venezuela Earthquakes: Country Appeal (July - December 2026)
passages.text: Venezuela is facing a major humanitarian emergency following two powerful earthquakes that struck on 24 June 2026. The states most affected include La Guaira, Distrito Capital, Miranda, Carabobo, Yaracuy, Falcón and neighbouring areas. The loss of livelihoods, disruption of health and protection services, and precarious living conditions—particularly for people residing in temporary shelters—are increasing the risk of gender-based violence and harmful coping mechanisms, especially among women, girls and adolescents. The health system is under severe strain. Many health facilities have sustained structural damage and are facing critical shortages of medicines, medical equipment and personnel, while disruptions to electricity, water supply and supply chains continue to hamper service delivery. To respond to the crisis, UNFPA is seeking US$10 million to scale up life-saving sexual and reproductive health services and strengthen gender-based violence prevention and response across the affected areas. UNFPA is targeting 64,000 people with life-saving sexual and reproductive health services, including emergency obstetric care, antenatal and postnatal care, neonatal care, testing and treatment for sexually transmitted infections, family planning services, clinical management of rape, and essential reproductive health information.

passages.title: UNFPA Situation Report: Earthquakes in Venezuela (24 June – 7 August 2026)
passages.text: Venezuela continues to face significant humanitarian needs following the earthquakes of 24 June 2026. The most urgent needs among affected populations include healthcare, including sexual and reproductive health (SRH); food and safe water; mental health and psychosocial support; shelter; sanitation and hygiene; and specialized protection services, particularly for gender-based violence (GBV). The loss of livelihoods, disruptions to health and protection services, and precarious living conditions—particularly for people residing in temporary shelters—are increasing the risk of GBV and harmful coping strategies. Currently, 24,477 people are residing in 107 transitional shelters, where overcrowding, limited privacy in sleeping and bathroom facilities, and inadequate lighting are heightening protection risks, particularly for women, girls, and adolescents. Numerous health facilities in affected areas have sustained structural damage, while others are facing shortages of medicines, equipment, and health personnel, placing additional strain on an already overstretched health system. UNFPA is supporting the continuity of life-saving maternal, newborn, and obstetric care through its support to maternity wards in 16 hospitals across La Guaira, Caracas, and Miranda. UNFPA is also providing on-the-job training for health personnel and delivering critical medical equipment and supplies, including 62 Inter-Agency Reproductive Health Kits, which will support the needs of approximately 2,250 people.

passages.title: Situation Report No.9: Earthquakes in Venezuela 2026 (M7.2 and M7.5), 12 August 2026
passages.text: **HIGHLIGHTS** Seven weeks after the two earthquakes that struck Venezuela on 24 June 2026, the response continues to sustain emergency operations while transitioning toward early recovery. Current efforts are focused on maintaining essential health services, rehabilitating affected facilities, supporting transitional camps, and delivering health services through a comprehensive approach, while mitigating public health risks and ensuring a continuous, needs-based supply of medicines and essential equipment. Health service recovery and critical care capacity are advancing, with rehabilitation planning progressing in priority facilities and intensive care and maternity capacity being restored at Hospital Dr. José Gregorio Hernández, while assessments in Caracas and Miranda continue to identify critical gaps in equipment and human resources. Public health surveillance and immunization systems are being reinforced, with expanded epidemiological analysis and digital reporting, enhanced laboratory diagnostic capacity, and more than 31,000 vaccine doses administered; national vaccine supply security was further supported through a USD 18 million Revolving Fund credit line. Efforts advanced toward the provision of comprehensive care, focusing on mental health, sexual and reproductive health, noncommunicable diseases, and rehabilitation. This included dissemination of the national mental health protocol, training of transitional camp focal points, continuity of oncology care through three designated centers, and attention to emerging needs such as assessing rehabilitation center capacities and training on amputee management and wound care. PAHO/WHO continued supporting the response with critical medicines and equipment, most recently delivering targeted emergency medical supplies – including specialized kits, medicines, and high-complexity surgical instruments – to the Maternal and Child Hospital Leopoldo Aguerrevere in Petare, Sucre.

Further funding contributions are needed to support the Venezuelan Red Cross in addressing the immediate, short- and medium-term needs of Venezuelans affected by the earthquakes. A. SITUATION ANALYSIS Description of the crisis On 24 June 2026, two powerful earthquakes struck north-central Venezuela in rapid succession; with the first one reaching a 7.2 magnitude, and a second one of 7.5 magnitude taking place approximately 39 seconds later. The epicentres were located near Morón and Yumare, in the states of Carabobo and Yaracuy, west of Caracas. USGS analysis confirmed the epicentre of the second earthquake to be approximately 17 km west of Catia La Mar, off the coast of La Guaira State1. Authorities have reported 1,463 aftershocks since the event, creating a high risk of further structural collapse2. The impact was severe and widespread, with tremors felt across much of the country, including the Capital District, La Guaira, Aragua, Carabobo, Miranda, Falcón, and neighbouring states. The earthquakes were also felt beyond Venezuela, including parts of Colombia, the Caribbean and northern Brazil, highlighting the exceptional geographic extent of the seismic event3. The Government of Venezuela declared a National State of Emergency the same day and designated La Guaira, where the greatest concentration of damaged infrastructure and rescue operations was concentrated, as a disaster zone.
